items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping organizational decision-making, yet its implications for ethical corporate conduct remain unclear. While AI may strengthen monitoring, improve compliance, and reduce opportunities for misconduct, it may also increase opacity, diffuse responsibility, and facilitate stakeholder-insensitive managerial behavior. We examine these competing possibilities by studying whether firm-level investment in AI-related human capital is associated with subsequent stakeholder-centric corporate misconduct (CM). Using a novel measure of AI-related employment and a large sample of U.S. public firms from 1999 to 2020, we find robust evidence that greater AI human capital investment is positively associated with future misconduct penalties. Economically, a one-standard deviation increase in AI investment corresponds to an approximately 19% increase in penalties in dollar terms. The relation remains robust across alternative measures, sensitivity tests, and instrumental variable analyses. Additional evidence shows that the association is concentrated in consumer protection, employment, and financial violations and is stronger among firms with opaque information environments and weaker governance structures. We further find that the adverse valuation consequences of misconduct are more pronounced among AI-intensive firms. Overall, our findings suggest that investments in AI-related human capital may create important ethical risks when not matched by effective oversight and accountability mechanisms. The study contributes to research on business ethics, corporate misconduct, and responsible AI governance.
items.title: Corporate Misconduct and Artificial Intelligence (AI): Ethical Cost of AI Adoption

items.abstract: Abstract Sufficiency has been receiving attention as a means to achieve sustainability. Insights on how to operationalise sufficiency in practice are limited and absent in the context of ecologically constrained organisations, such as, charities. Charities are viewed as critical to sustainability due to their reuse business model; however, charity income is dropping due to the saturation of low-quality and value clothing donations generated by ever-increasing production and consumption of (ultra)fast fashion. This is placing resource (e.g. reliance on volunteer labour) and ecological (e.g. finding reuse routes) burdens on an already constrained sector, highlighting the urgency for charities to future proof the retail businesses foundational to their fundraising efforts. To address this challenge, this research adopts an ethic of sufficiency to introduce business model innovation to charity retail. Drawing on interviews and observations with charity staff, collaborating experts and consumers as donor and retail users, we examine transition to a clothing rental model offering social and ecological sufficiency. We find that the two competing ethics of: (1) sufficiency representing enough and driving deceleration and (2) insufficiency representing not enough and driving acceleration, compete for primacy. While sufficiency can counter challenges arising from insufficiency, competition between them creates contradictory pressures for the charity. This is further exasperated by a misalignment between organisation and consumer experiences of sufficiency. The theoretical and practical implications of the findings for sufficiency, charity retail, rental and consumption are discussed.
items.title: Sustainability in Charity Retail: Conflicts in (In)Sufficiency

items.abstract: Abstract Integrity is one of the key concepts in business ethics and has conventionally been understood as a quality of the autonomous ethical subject. Relational approaches have challenged this view by showing how integrity is shaped through everyday human encounters and organisational practices. Feminist post-humanist thinking takes this challenge further by questioning human-centred understandings of ethical subjectivity itself. Drawing on Karen Barad’s articulations of entanglement and diffraction, this paper explores what happens to integrity when ethical subjectivity is understood as emerging through more-than-human entanglements. Through a collaborative diffractive reading of theoretical discussions on integrity and entanglement, alongside a sustainability manager’s empirical account, we trace three recurring patterns of entangled subjectivity: sensing that something is not right, carrying the weight of responsibility, and aspiring towards more liveable entanglements. These patterns show how integrity comes to matter through embodied, affective, material, and organisational entanglements. Building on these patterns, this research develops ‘entangrity’ as a relational and lively reconceptualisation of integrity, understood as an expression of entangled subjectivity. Entangrity renews questions surrounding ambiguous ethical subjectivities by pointing to the way ethical tensions are dwelt within, rather than ‘navigated’. It also exemplifies how diffractive reading can enable conceptual development whilst keeping different and even ontologically distinct theoretical perspectives in play. Thus, we invite thinking-with the possibilities of what ethical subjectivity and response-ability might become as posthuman business ethics continues to be developed.
items.title: From Integrity to Entangrity: A Diffractive Reading of a Sustainability Manager’s Entangled Subjectivity

items.abstract: Abstract We argue that contemporary chatbots participate in conversations without making assertions, but instead by performing proto-assertoric acts (in a sense to be explicated) that are sensitive to the evolving needs of interlocutors, and in ways that help a conversation achieve its goal. In support of this claim we distinguish among different proto-assertoric stages including what we call ursertions and semisertions. These are utterances that can be evaluated for correctness while falling short of the epistemic and normative commitments characteristic of assertion. When appropriately sensitive to a shared conversational task, such utterances can nevertheless advance that task. We deploy this framework by treating conversations as goal-directed enterprises aimed at resolving practical or theoretical questions, within which such proto-assertoric interventions can play a substantive role. This account explains in a principled way how chatbots can participate in conversations without thereby attributing to them sensitivity to the distinctive normative commitments associated with assertion.
items.title: Conversing without asserting: chatbots as interlocutors

items.abstract: It has become increasingly popular to distinguish two types of weight that reasons can have: one connected in some way to the overall status of being required, the other to the overall status of being justified or permitted. The purpose of this essay is to argue that this distinction between “requiring weight” and “justifying weight” is not in good standing. Attempts to motivate such a distinction through an appeal to two parallel definitions of what it is for a reason to have each type of weight fail, because a reason’s weight cannot be defined in terms of the conditions under which an action or attitude has (or is made to have, or is pushed toward having) a given status at the overall level. And attempts to motivate such a distinction by extracting it from substantive proposals about how reasons combine in order to yield overall verdicts also fail, because, among other problems, such proposals lead to wildly implausible first-order verdicts. Although how reasons and their weights play off each other in the determination of what, all things considered, to do (or think, or feel) is potentially a very complicated affair, we lack good reason to think the weights of reasons neatly sort into two piles, one of a distinctively requiring sort, the other of a peculiarly justifying variety.
items.title: A Reason Itself Neither Requires nor Permits: On an Alleged Distinction between Two Roles for Reasons

items.abstract: Abstract Recent years have seen increasing concern that artificial intelligence may soon pose an existential risk to humanity. One leading ground for concern is that artificial agents may be power-seeking, aiming to acquire power and in the process disempowering humanity. I show how the argument from power-seeking rests on a strong version of a claim known as the instrumental convergence thesis. I explore leading defenses of the instrumental convergence thesis and argue that none establishes the thesis in a strong enough form to ground the argument from power-seeking. I discuss implications for longtermism, the governance of artificial intelligence, and the methodology of studying risks posed by artificial agents.
items.title: Instrumental convergence and power seeking

items.abstract: Abstract The April 2025 integration of Ipsotek’s AI-driven video analytics software into Raptor Alert’s emergency management platform marks a significant escalation in the deployment of facial recognition technologies across U.S. public schools. Through a synthesis of Huey P. Newton’s (1972) theory of bureaucratic capitalism and the interpretive paradigm of Black Male Studies (Curry, 2017), this paper provides a clarifying framework for understanding the counterinsurgent logics at play within AI-augmented school surveillance regimes and their historically entrenched consequences for Black male students. By situating Raptor Alert’s implementation within Victor Rios’s (2011) account of the youth control complex, the paper introduces the analytic device of the potential gang member (PGM) to theorize the institutional mutation of the military-aged male (MAM) category identified by Clay-Gilmore (2025) within educational settings. Lastly, factoring in recent empirical findings that attest to the presence of racial bias in facial recognition algorithms, alongside the historically sustained and disproportionately punitive disciplinary measures enacted upon Black male students in U.S. public schools, we argue that the emergence of an educational milieu in which technologization algorithmically formalizes the androcentric patterns of target acquisition deeply entrenched in American society, collapsing the boundaries between the carceral and the educational under the aegis of technocratic governance, demands that we abandon the reformist metaphor of the “school-to-prison pipeline” in favor of the explanatory hermeneutic of the “school-as-prison.”
items.title: Automated nihility: Huey P. Newton, Raptor Alert, and the bureaucratic capitalism of surveillance in U.S. public schools

items.abstract: Abstract The goal of this paper is to offer an analysis of causation in terms of explanation. The basis of the analysis is a plausible principle about “cause-tracing explanations”, i.e. explanations that cite causes: c causes e if and only if the fact that c causes e explains the fact that c explains e. I use this principle to develop an analysis of causation in terms of the role it plays in explanation. I then offer three arguments for my “explanationist” analysis: it scores well on the desideratum of parsimony; it answers the question of what distinguishes grounding from causation; and finally, it offers a compelling synthesis of two seemingly incompatible pictures of explanation and explanatory relations.
items.title: An explanationist analysis of causation

items.abstract: Abstract This paper provides an account of radical deviance, of what a speaker must do that would require us to translate her words non-homophonically. The account comes in two parts. The first argues that the appropriate unit of analysis for radical deviance is not a speaker’s utterance of individual sentences considered in isolation from her dealings with other speakers, but her contribution to a meaning-giving dialectic considered as a whole. The second argues that a speaker’s use of a word counts as radically deviant if only if it involves a refusal either (1) to engage in or (2) to respect the meaning-giving dialectic for that word. This account has two important consequences. First, it resolves a longstanding issue with semantic externalism, namely, that of explaining what a speaker must do to get thrown out of the social practice her participation in which secures for her words the meanings they have. Second, it provides a new contribution to the debate over the understanding-assent links thesis, according to which some sentences p are such that, necessarily, whoever understands p assents to p. Williamson (2007, 2012/2020) has argued that there are no such links. Boghossian (2012/2020) and Warren (2021) take themselves to have provided counterexamples to Williamson’s argument. Whether one considers these counterexamples to be genuine, however, is a matter of intuition. Thus the debate is at an impasse. The account of radical deviance proposed here provides a way out.
items.title: Escaping the understanding-assent links impasse

items.abstract: Matthew McGrath and Jane Friedman provided great comments on Knowledge: A Human Interest Story . Here I reply to them, making some concessions, and relying on a distinction I wish I’d drawn in the book. The distinction is between inquiries that aim at finding something out, and inquiries that aim at checking something. These two inquiries relate differently to knowledge. Any knowledge one has is fair game to use as a starting point to finding things out, but there are different constraints on how you check things. Making this distinction allows for a cleaner statement of the role of knowledge in certain kinds of inquiry, i.e., findings out, while allowing that knowers can sensibly check what they already know.
items.title: Reply to commentators

items.abstract: In Knowledge: A Human Interest Story , I argue for an interest-relative theory of knowledge. The argument rests on principles connecting knowledge and action, combined with some judgments about which actions are rational in a particular low-stakes game. In this short piece, I set out that argument, and highlight the distinctive features of version of interest-relativity I defend: that odds rather than stakes matter to knowledge; that merely hypothetical and theoretical questions can change what one knows; that questions about what to do must be separated from questions about what maximises expected utility; and that knowledge is a constraint on the starting points of inquiry, not its endings.
items.title: Précis of knowledge: a human interest story

items.abstract: Abstract I show that a standard argument against the possibility of a valid Dutch book argument for countable additivity is too quick because it fails to distinguish different notions of convergence for random variables. Making this distinction allows for the precise formulation of such a Dutch book argument.
items.title: Countable Dutch Book Arguments

items.abstract: Abstract Mental imagery appears to be an essentially private phenomenon, and, for that reason, ill-suited to play a genuinely interpersonal role. This paper argues that intersubjective coordination of mental imagery is possible without sharing token imagistic representations. I distinguish two senses in which mental imagery might be shared and argue that neither is required for imagistic coordination. Imagistic cognition can be coordinated across agents without requiring shared mental images or fully identical contents, provided that their imagistic activities are governed by shared constraints and guided by common commitments. Drawing on work on shared perception and joint action, I contend that privacy at the level of mental tokens and phenomenal character does not preclude the interpersonal coordination of mental imagery in a functionally relevant sense.
items.title: Coordinating Mental Imagery

items.abstract: Scientists from the People’s Republic of China have become increasingly active in global climate change research. Using a mix of quantitative and qualitative sources, we show that the international scientific publications in the field of climate change by Chinese scholars increased rapidly after 2010 and overtook publications by scientists from the United States in 2023. This rise in international publications was related to important policies of support by the Chinese government, including improved access to research funding. It was also reflected in Chinese policies addressing the challenges of climate change and air pollution, such as reductions in carbon emissions via carbon capture technologies, which promise to mitigate future effects of climate change in China.
items.title: China’s Climate Change Science and Policies
